paras: The killing of J. E. Martin was the murder of a merchant at Belknap, Texas, who was called from his house by three men on the night of June 9, 1881, led about half a mile away and shot dead. The men then robbed his store, and about two weeks later three men named McDonald were jailed at Graham for the crime amid fears that Belknap citizens would lynch them.

Martin was described as a prominent merchant of Belknap, and no report gave his race or any accusation against him. The Graham correspondent noted that the heaviest storm of the season struck that evening, with hail and about three inches of rain in under two hours.

According to a Graham special to the Dallas Herald, three unknown men called Martin out of his residence about 8 o'clock at night and led him off about half a mile, where they shot him to death. Another account said he was called to the door, seized and carried a short distance from the house before he was shot. The men then went to his store, took all they could carry and escaped under cover of the storm.

Sheriff Melton and several deputies left Graham for Belknap the next morning in search of the robbers, and citizens offered a reward of two thousand dollars for their capture. On June 25 a Graham dispatch reported that Melton and Deputy U.S. Marshal Connor had captured three men in Coleman county and were bringing them to Graham.

By June 27 the sheriff had lodged Pete, D. and Nick McDonald in the Graham jail, after finding them asleep at a father's house with goods recognized as stolen and seven horses said to be stolen in Grayson county. A large number of people from Belknap had come to Graham, and the dispatch said it was feared an attempt would be made to lynch the prisoners. No report of a lynching attempt, an inquest or a trial appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers mainly through two specials from Graham: one to the Dallas Herald and one relayed by the St. Louis Republican, which papers in Nevada, Wyoming, Tennessee and West Virginia reprinted within days. Headlines framed it as frontier crime, such as the Gold Hill Daily News's "Bold Murder and Robbery" and the Savannah Morning News's "Crime in Texas. Murder and Robbery Under Cover of a Storm." Shorter versions ran as single lines in crime roundups, one of which, in the Watertown Republican, described the men as "masked" and omitted the robbery.

The arrest reports, carried from Richmond to Wilmington and Concord, called the McDonalds the men "who murdered Mr. Martin" without qualification. They gave the threat of mob action a prominent place, as in the Delaware State Journal's headline "Under Arrest in a Texas Town and in Danger of Lynching," without comment on it.

The Graham dispatches place the killing on the night of June 9, while the Watertown roundup gave the date as the 10th, the date on the earliest Graham dispatch. Versions of the jailing report differ on one prisoner's name, "D." or "Dine" McDonald, and on whether they were caught at the house of the father of two of them or of all three.

reader.title: Killing of J. E. Martin
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: The papers describe a robbery-murder: three men called a merchant from his house, shot him and robbed his store, with no mob, no accusation against the victim and no race stated (A5, A9, A15).

Martin was killed illegally by three men (A9, A5), but the reports give robbery, not any claim of justice, race or tradition, as the circumstance, and the men then robbed his store (A5, A9); the only lynching talk concerns feared mob action against the arrested suspects, which no report shows happening (A11, A15).

Two separately sent Graham specials, one to the Dallas Herald and one carried from Galveston, agree on the calling out, the shooting half a mile away and the store robbery (A9, A5), and later Graham dispatches report the capture and jailing of suspects (A11, A14).

framing.detail: Papers outside Texas ran the Graham specials under crime headlines such as 'Bold Murder and Robbery' and 'Crime in Texas', or as one-line items in crime roundups.
Arrest reports called the prisoners 'the murderers' outright and stressed the danger that they would be lynched, without comment on it ('Under Arrest in a Texas Town and in Danger of Lynching').

versions.value: Night of June 9 ('last night' in a June 10 Graham dispatch; 'night before last' in a June 11 one; 'Thursday')

conflicts.note: The Graham dispatch dated June 10 is local and earliest, so June 9 is better supported; the roundup's 'the 10th' likely took the dispatch date.
Only the Watertown roundup says the men were masked; the Graham dispatches do not.
